description: Psoriasis is a common, chronic, inflammatory and proliferative condition of the skin and may be associated with systemic manifestations in many organ systems. The most characteristic lesions are red, scaly, sharply demarcated, indurated plaques, particularly over the extensor surfaces and scalp. It can cause itching, irritation, burning and stinging, and the extent and severity vary enormously over time and between individuals. In Ayurveda, psoriasis corresponds broadly to Kustha, aligning with subtypes such as EkaKustha, Kitibha, Sidhma, Vipadika, Mandala, Pundarika and Carmadala, involving predominance of Vata-Kapha in plaque types, Pitta-Kapha in pustular forms, and Vata-Pitta in psoriatic arthritis.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Psoriasis vulgaris is a chronic, non-communicable, disfiguring, and disabling disease with negative impact of varied degree on a patient's quality of life (QoL). It affects males and females equally. About 2–3% of the population have psoriasis and 10% of these individuals will develop psoriatic arthritis. Of this group, in 3–5% of them, it is severe. According to the World Health Organization, approximately 0.09% - 11.43% (incidence 46,22,594, prevalence 4,08,05,386) of the global population suffers from psoriasis. In India, the prevalence of this illness varies from 0.44 to 2.8%; both sexes affected equally with few studies showing male predominance and most of the patients are in their third or fourth decade at the time of presentation. The lifetime risk of developing the disease is strongly associated with a family history; if no parent has psoriasis, the risk is 4%; if one parent has psoriasis, the risk is 14-28% and if both parents have psoriasis, the risk is 40-65%.

sections.title: Pathogenesis & Therapeutic Implications
sections.content: 1. Genetics: There are two peaks of onset of psoriasis (Fig.). Type I has onset in the second and third decades and a more common family history of psoriasis. Type II has onset in late adulthood in patients without obvious family history. 2. Hyperproliferation: The growth fraction of the upper layer of skin known as the epidermis is increased with the basal cell being increased 7x compared with normal skin. The cell turnover time decreases from 30 to 5 days, similarly the cell cycle time reduces from 311 to 36 hours. 3. Inflammation: Psoriasis is now known to be an autoimmune disorder with CD4 T cells, Th17 and Th 22 cells playing an important role. Notably these cells are determined by cytokines that are the target of novel drugs known as biologics which have changed the therapeutics of psoriasis. Psoriatic keratinocytes contain high levels of antimicrobial peptides which may account for the surprisingly low incidence of bacterial skin infection. 4. Psoriasis is also now appreciated to be an intimate part of the metabolic syndrome, associated with hypertension, diabetes mellitus, and coronary artery disease.

sections.title: Ayurvedic Correlation
sections.content: In Ayurveda, psoriasis corresponds broadly to Kustha, a term for chronic skin diseases caused by dosha-dhatu-mala imbalances and systemic disturbances. Psoriasis aligns with subtypes such as EkaKustha, Kitibha, Sidhma, Vipadika, Mandala, Pundarika and Carmadala, involving predominance of Vata-Kapha in plaque types, Pitta-Kapha in pustular forms, and Vata-Pitta in psoriatic arthritis. The pathogenesis (Samprapti) includes dietary and lifestyle factors causing impaired digestion (Agni), accumulation of toxins (Ama), and obstruction of channels (Srotorodha), paralleling immune dysregulation and systemic inflammation. Ayurveda also recognizes the systemic nature of psoriasis through its holistic view of Kustha, linking it to chronic metabolic and psychological imbalances. Comorbidities like cardiovascular disorders, metabolic syndrome, and depression are conceptualized as manifestations of Dushivisha (chronic toxins), Mandagni (impaired digestive fire), and Avarana Vata (obstruction in channels), emphasizing the need for comprehensive management addressing physical and mental health. This integrated understanding supports the use of Shodhana (detoxification), Shamana (palliative treatment), Rasayana (rejuvenation), and Satvavajaya (psychological therapies) to address both cutaneous lesions and systemic complications effectively.

sections.title: Clinical Presentation
sections.content: Psoriasis has several clinical variants that differ in severity, location, longevity, shape, cause and pattern. The course of the disease is marked by exacerbations and remissions usually get worse in winters. Patients may experience more than one type of Psoriasis at the same time. Table 02: Ayurvedic Correlates of different types of Psoriasis and their Features — Plaque Psoriasis (Sharply demarcated red to salmon-pink plaques with silvery-white scales; symmetrical; common on elbows, knees, scalp, sacrum) → Charma Kustha, Vata-Kapha dominance; rough dry skin → EkaKustha, Kitibha. Guttate Psoriasis (Acute onset, numerous small drop-like papules (1–10 mm) mainly on trunk and limbs; often post-strep infection) → Padmapatra lesions; toxin-induced origin → Sudden eruption, Kustha, Visha toxin (visha) or Janya infection cause. Flexural Psoriasis (Smooth, erythematous patches with minimal scaling in skin folds (axillae, groin, inframammary)) → Smooth, Parimandala/Mandala moist, soft patches → Pitta-Kapha predominance. Pustular Psoriasis (Generalized sterile pustules on erythematous base; systemic symptoms (fever, malaise)) → Thick pus, burning sensation → Pundarika, Visarpa vitiation; thick pus accumulation → Pitta-Kapha. Palmoplantar Pustulosis (Painful pustules localized to palms and soles) → Painful, pustular eruptions → Vipadika Kshudra Kustha; severe local discomfort. Erythrodermic Psoriasis (Extensive redness and scaling (>75–90% BSA); systemic symptoms (fever, chills)) → Severe inflammation with systemic signs → Carmadalam, Oudumbara, Visarpa → Pitta-Kapha. Nail Psoriasis (Nail pitting, oil spots, subungual hyperkeratosis, onycholysis) → Nail deformities → Kunakha → Vatadosha involvement causing nail changes. Scalp Psoriasis & Sebopsoriasis (Flaky, greasy scales on scalp, hairline, nasolabial folds) → Kapha-Pitta dominant; Arumshaka → Thick greasy scales resembling feathers (viluna pakshavat). Psoriatic Arthritis (Joint pain, stiffness, swelling; dactylitis; DIP and spine involvement) → Vata and rakta vitiation → Vatasonitha Poorvarupa → Vata dominance; affects rakta, asthi (bone) and sandhi (joints).

sections.title: Clinical Examination
sections.content: Psoriasis is mostly diagnosed on the basis of clinical examination of the skin, scalp, and nails along with review of patient's smoking history, medical history and family history. The characteristic skin lesions are sharply demarcated, scaly, erythematous raised plaques, either painful or itching red patches covered with silvery scales. The lesions vary in shape and may be ovoid, round, or irregular and are often symmetrically distributed. Common areas of involvement include extensor surface of body, elbows, knees, scalp, trunk, lumbosacral region and nails. A skin biopsy is needed in some cases to confirm the diagnosis and to rule out other diseases. Ayurveda clinical examination comprises of Darshana, Sparshana and Prashna Pareeksha which provides leads to dosha predominance of clinical manifestation of psoriasis. Dashavidha Pareeksha (Tenfold examination) are also included in Ayurveda clinical examination to formulate adequate treatment protocol.

sections.title: Investigations
sections.content: Supportive Investigations: Diagnosing psoriasis is typically based on clinical presentation. A skin biopsy will be helpful in atypical cases. In generalized pustular psoriasis, high sensitivity C-reactive protein may be mildly elevated, but higher levels are seen in psoriatic arthritis. Blood tests like CBC (Complete Blood Count), KFT (Kidney Function Test), LFT (Liver Function Test), HLA B27 (Human Leukocyte Antigen B27), Uric acid levels, Human Immunodeficiency Virus, Rheumatoid factor, X-ray and Antinuclear antibodies, tests for specific infections like streptococcal and staphylococcal antibodies can help differentiate psoriasis from other conditions with similar symptoms. KOH preparation should be done to rule out fungal infection (Tinea etc) in cases of psoriasis of hands, feet, and nails. Table 06: Tests for diagnosis — 1) Bedside tests: a) Grattage test - positive when scales are accentuated by grating lesions with a glass slide. b) Auspitz sign - When gently scraping off all the scales from lesions with a glass slide, a glistening white adherent membrane (Berkley's membrane) appears. Once this membrane is removed, punctate bleeding points become visible. (positive Auspitz sign). 2) Skin biopsy - Skin biopsy (done in doubtful cases) shows epidermis and dermal changes. Epidermal changes include parakeratosis, absent granular layer, regular acanthosis, suprapapillary thinning, elongation of rete ridges and collection of neutrophils in the epidermis (spongiform pustule of Kogoj and Munro's microabscess). Dermal changes: dilatation and tortuosity of capillary loops in dermal papillae, and lymphocyte infiltrates in the upper dermis.

sections.title: Ayurvedic Diagnosis
sections.content: Ayurveda Diagnosis: Lakshana: Lesions with Khara sparsa (Plaque like lesion); Lesion with Rajah kiret (Fine powdery scales), Matsyashakala sannibha (Silvery Scales); Mandala (chronic Patch like lesion); Presence of lakshanas like Kandu / Daha / Ruja; Location of lesions; Nakha dushti (Psoriatic nail changes); Presence of Arthritis (vatasonitham); Nimitta alpe api kopanam – Kobners phenomenon; Chronic lesions – Chirasthithi. Dosha assessment: Table 07 — Key Ayurvedic Features: Dry, rough (Khina khara sparsham) → Kitibha → Vata-Kapha; Fish-scale-like lesions (Matsya shakala sannibham) → EkaKustha; Rough, Dark color → Charma Kustha (Hasticharma khara sparsham); Dew drop appearance (Padmapatra eva amsubhi) sudden onset; toxin/infection-related → Pundarika → Kapha-pitta; Smooth, moist, circular Patch like lesion → Parimandala/Mandala Kustha → Pitta-Kapha; Thick, hot pustules; burning sensation → Pundarika, Visarpa; Painful pustular eruptions with severe itching in palms and soles → Vipadika → Vata-Kapha; Pitta-Kapha; Severe redness, swelling, systemic symptoms (intensely aggravated) → Carmadalam, Oudumbara, Visarpa (severe forms); Nail pitting, onycholysis, nail deformities → Kunakha → Vata; Greasy, thick, feather-like scaling → Sidhma Kustha → Kapha-Pitta; Joint involvement; bone pain; pre-arthritic phase & Sandhi → Vatasonitha Poorvarupa → Vata (affecting Asthi). Classification of severity and prognostic assessment: Psoriasis area severity index (PASI) score — The PASI is a widely used instrument in psoriasis trials that assesses and grades the severity of psoriatic lesions and the patient's response to treatment. It produces a numeric score ranging from 0 to 72. A 75% reduction in the PASI score (PASI 75) is the current benchmark for most clinical trials. Nail psoriasis Severity index (NAPSI) — This scale is used to evaluate the severity of nail bed psoriasis and nail matrix psoriasis by area of involvement in the nail unit.

sections.title: Principles of Management
sections.content: The principles of management include assessment of signs and symptoms before initiating treatment and the need for management through conventional treatment for associated comorbidities. If the patient is already under standard conventional care, the physician may advice to continue the same along with add-on Ayurvedic treatment and can assess/consider for tapering or discontinue the treatment in the follow ups. Must check about the intake of drugs that can trigger or exaggerate psoriasis in the history of the patient. According to Ayurveda, Kustha is a disease that arises due to improper diet and lifestyle (mithya ahara and vihara), along with certain causative factors (nidana) that also impact psychological aspects. So, in the management of psoriasis, both prevention and curative aspects concentrate on diet, life style and psychological component. Shodhana: As per Ayurveda classical literature, Shodhana chikitsa is indicated in bahudosha. The 'Shodhana' will be followed by rasayana protocol which aims at stabilizing dhathu which helps to prevent recurrence. Shamana: Shamana therapy is primarily indicated in conditions with madhya (moderate) or alpa (mild) dosha dushti. Assessment of bahu, madhyama, and alpa dosha can be integrated with objective parameters—for example, the PASI (area and erythema–induration–desquamation scores), overall severity of clinical features, and the vulnerability/functional significance of the involved sites (e.g., face, genitals, palms/soles, nail unit, flexures). Shamana therapy involves both internal and external formulations, such as kwatha, arishta, churna, ghrita, taila, and lepa. In psoriasis, bahirparimarjana chikitsa (external therapy) is particularly beneficial when the vitiated doshas are cleared at the level of deeper dhathus and get localized at the level of the twak (skin). In cases of bahu dosha avastha (excessive dosha aggravation), Shamana chikitsa is administered after Shodhana therapy, to pacify the remaining doshas. Satvavajaya: Satvavajaya chikitsa or psychotherapy in Ayurveda is indicated through dhee, dhairya and atmaadi vijnaanam. This has a major role in correcting psoriatic complications including psoriatic depression.

sections.title: Red Flag Signs
sections.content: These signs should be assessed before initiating treatment for need for management through modern medicine: Patients with generalized pustular psoriasis or erythrodermic psoriasis with high grade fever; Psoriatic arthritis significantly impacting a person's physical, psychological or social well-being; Psoriasis with comorbid disorders.

sections.title: Preventive Treatment
sections.content: (A) Prevention Management: Diet: Ayurveda dietary directives termed as Aṣṭāhāra-vidhi-viśeṣa principles are essential in diet planning for prevention of psoriasis for high-risk group patients. It is also advised that one's satmya ahara (habitual, agreeable food) be served warm, fresh, neither overly dry nor heavy, and consumed mindfully with thorough chewing at a measured pace. Life style: Ayurveda emphasizes adherence to dinacharya (daily routine) and ritucharya (seasonal routine), with particular attention to following dinacharya in the correct sequence. Yoga: Various yoga practices may be helpful in the management of psoriasis, such as Shavasana (Corpse Pose), Bhujangasana (Cobra pose), Setu Bandhasana (Bridge Pose), Trikonasana (Triangle Pose), Balasana (Child's Pose). Certain Pranayam and meditation techniques like Anulom Vilom (Alternate Nostril Breathing), Bhramari (Humming Bee Breath), and Kapalbhati (Skull Shining Breath) will also help in reducing anxiety, emotional stress, cellular healing, reducing stress-related inflammation and promoting a positive mental state.

sections.title: Treatment Levels
sections.content: Level 1: Solo physician clinic/health clinic/PHC (Optimal standard of treatment where technology and resources are limited). Psoriasis cases with mild to moderate severity, BSA<10 can be treated in level 1. BSA>10, non-responding cases of mild to moderate severity and severe cases shall be referred to level 2 and 3. The varieties of psoriasis like guttate, erythrodermic psoriasis, generalized pustular psoriasis, psoriasis with co-morbidities, associated depression, cardiometabolic risks may also be referred to level 2 and 3. Fastly spreading psoriasis with acuteness of symptoms as in visarpa, where continuous monitoring is needed shall be referred to level 2 and 3. Psoriasis with bahu doshavastha with recurrences and relapses shall be also referred to level 2 and 3. Clinical diagnosis: Psoriasis is entirely diagnosed clinically with thorough medical history and physical examination, including BMI. However, some investigations, such as complete hemogram, urine routine/microscopic, C-reactive protein, fasting blood sugar, postprandial blood sugar levels, and serum uric acid levels can be advised. Management: Prevention protocol: Diet: Ayurveda based dietary advisories for prevention of skin disease can be followed as part of primary prevention. Lifestyle: Life style advocacies based on Ayurveda sleep regimen, vegadharana, promotion of vyayama, following proper dinacharya with udwarthana therapy (powder massage) and ritucharya to prevent seasonal exacerbations. Curative Intervention: At level 1, curative intervention is solely based on Shamana protocol based on dosha predominance of clinical manifestation. Plaque psoriasis – Vata kapha Kustha (charma Kustha, eka Kustha, kitibha): In active phase (pro-inflammatory phase), Manjishtadi kwatha, Punarnavadi kwatha, Vilwadi gutika, Dooshivishari gutika, Arogya vardhini gutika, Avipatti churna, Nishunti shadanga (Shadanga excluding sunthi), Chandrakala Rasa etc can be advocated. Mahamanjishtadi kwatha and Patolakaturohinyadi kwatha can be given in the sub acute phase. Ayyappala kera taila, Dinesavalyadi kera oil, Jeevanthyadi yamaka, Vajraka ghrtha and Mahātikta Ghṛta can be advocated as Shamana medicine in vatakapha phase. The external applications shall be withheld in the pittanubandha conditions as in acute phase and shall be only applied after inflammation has been subsided. Guttate psoriasis, Generalized Pustular psoriasis, Inverse psoriasis- Pittakapha pradhana Kustha: pittakapha hara kashayas like Vasaguloochyadi and Padolamooladi kashayam are preferred choices, alongside Avipatti choornam, Amritashadanga panakam, Kaisora guggulu and Amrita guggulu. In non-exudative phase Durvaditaila, Nalpamarditaila etc. can be used externally. In case of associated Jwara, Sudarshana Gutika and Mustaparpataka panakam can be added. Thiktaka ghrita and Mahathiktaka ghrita can be advocated when active phase of inflammation is over. Note: If Ama is either minimal or addressed with brief deepana–pachana, a small, supervised samana-sneha of Mahatikta Ghrta / Tiktaka Ghṛta / Pancatiktaka Ghrta (≈ 10 mL, b.i.d.) is beneficial even in acute phases. Palmoplantar psoriasis – Treatment principle of vipadika can be adopted. In exudative and bleeding phase, the medicines mentioned in acute phase of vata kapha Kustha can be used. In dry vata kapha phases, non-exudative non-painful presentation, medicines mentioned in sub-acute/chronic phases can be advocated. The external applications in subacute and chronic phases include jeevanthyadi yamaka and mahathiktaka ghrita lepa. Scalp psoriasis: The treatment principle is similar to plaque psoriasis. External scalp applications include Ayyappala kera taila and durvadi taila. Psoriatic arthritis (Vatarakta): It is seen associated in 30% of psoriasis cases. The treatment principle includes the treatment protocol of plaque psoriasis and vatarakta treatment protocol including Mahamanjishtadi kwatha, shaddharanam churna/tablet and Simhanada guggulu for arthritic management. Manibhadra gula can be used internally in all varieties of psoriasis when active inflammatory phase is over.

sections.title: Purification Procedures
sections.content: Since purificatory procedures like vamana and virechana require Shodhana snehapana under strict medical supervision, in level 1, feasibility issues will be there for implementation of Shodhana protocol. Sadya snehapana followed by sadyovamana, siravedha can be planned in OPD basis under strict medical supervision. Level 2 Shodhana: Deepana and pachana- with Shaddharana churna or Hingwashtakachurna or Vaishwanarachurna or Ajamojadichurna or Bhaskara lavanachurna - 3-6 twice daily before food or Chitrakadi gutika. for a duration of 3 days or till the patient have good appetite. Snehapana- with Panchatiktakaghrita or Aragwadhaghrita or Tiktakaghrita or Mahatiktakaghrita - starting from 30 ml till samyaksnigdha lakshana (in arohana doses increased according to agni). Duration of 3 to 7 days. Sadya snehapana is indicated in children and adolescents. Abhyanga and Swedana- Eladi kera or Nalpamaraditaila or Nimbaditaila or any suitable oil as per dosha involvement indicated for Kustha or twakroga followed by ushnambusnana. Duration of 3 days. Vamana- with Madanapippali, Nimba, Vacha, Saindhava and Madhu (or) Vacha Yashtimadhu Madanapippali in Nimba swarasa with honey (or) Any vamana yoga specifically indicated for skin disease. Duration: One day. Samsarjana krama- Peyadi karma as per avara, madhyama or pravarashuddhi for 3/5/7 days. Virechana- with Nimbamritadiera ndataila, Avipattikara churna or Avipatti choorna, Trivrit choorna or Triphala kwatha or other virechana drugs according to the dosha predominance. Other internal medicines are stopped during virechana and restarted during or after samsarjana krama. Samsarjana krama after virechana as per avara, madhyama or pravarashuddhi for 3/5/7 days. During snehapana, vamana, virechana and samsarjana krama period other internal medicines are stopped. Sarvanga Kashaya dhara. With Aragwadhadikashaya or Manjishtadikashaya or Panchatiktaka Kashaya or any twakdoshahara and raktaprasadana kashaya. Takradhara- with Musta Amalaki takra or Aragwadhaditakra or Manjishtaditakra or Panchatiktakatakra for 7 days. Takradhara may be extended to 14 or 21 days as per dosha status. In children, Shirolepam may be done instead of dhara. When shirolepam is done, amalaki and buttermilk prepared in kashayasiddha ksheera are used and Talam is also done with Rasnadi or Kachuradichurna with Dhanvantaram taila or Bala taila or Nimbamritaditaila. Prachhana/ Raktamokshana/ Siravedha: As per locations of lesions on lalata, hasta pada or shiras. Prachana is done in alpadosha status. In bahudosha, Siravedha is advised. Jalooka can be applied in children. All internal medicines are continued till dosha and rogashamana also considering upashayaanupashaya. Rasayana drugs are started after dosha and rogashamana and continued for a period of one to 6 months. Ayurvediya Swasthavritta is to be followed during treatment and continued after complete rogashamana.

sections.title: Rasayana
sections.content: Table No: 10 List of Rasayana drugs that can be used in the treatment of Psoriasis — Gandhaka rasayana (Tablets, 250-500 mg daily, after food, Twice daily, After dosha and rogashamana as rasayana (for a period of one to 6 months)), Tuvaraka Rasayana (Tuvaraka rasayana, 10-20 drops, Once daily, Rasayana, Goksheera/Ghee/butter), Bhallataka Rasayana (Avaleha, ½ to 1 g, For Bhallataka rasayana, Ghrita, madhu), Yasada Bhasma (Bhasma, 100mg, Twice daily, As rasayana), Madhusnuhi Rasayana (Avaleha, 10-15 g daily after food, Once daily, After dosha and rogashamana as rasayana (for a period of one to 6 months)). Rasayana chikitsa should be done in all cases for preventing recurrence (apunarbhava) which is very common in psoriasis due to involvement of autoimmunity (ojovisramsa). Rasayana drugs are started after dosha and rogashamana and continued for a period of one to 6 months.

sections.title: Pathya-Apathya
sections.content: Table No. 08: Pathya-Apathya (Do's & Don'ts) for Kushtha (Skin Disorders). All Kustha nidana can be treated as apathya since treatment itself is nidana parivarjanam. Pathya/Do's: Laghu anna (Light food); Tikta shaka (green leafy vegetables); Ghrita (Ghrita); Mudga (Green gram); Aadaki (Pigeon pea); Masoora (Red lentil); Yava (barley); Godhooma (wheat); Madhu (Honey); Sali (Rice); Karkati (Cucumber); Patola (Snake gourd); Nimbapatra (Neem leaves); Tila Taila (gingelly oil); Sarshapa taila (Mustard oil); Tila (sesame); Dravasnigdhaguru Ahara (liquid, unctuous and heavy to digest food). Apathya/Don'ts: Dugdha (milk); Dadhi (curd); Kulatha (horse gram); Masha (black gram); Nishpava (green peas); Ikshu (sugarcane); Amla Rasa (sour fruits); Virudha Ahara (incompatible food); Adhyasana (taking another meal before the earlier one is digested); Ajeerna (indigestion); Vishamasana (untimely food); Vidahi (burning sensation), vishtambhi and Abhishyandi ahara; Matsya (fish); Guda (jaggery). Vihara-Apathya: Vegavaraodha (Suppression of natural urges); Atapasevana (Over exposure to Sun); Drinking cold water after direct exposure to the sun and after exertion; Day sleep; Stress; Doing exercise or over exertion immediately after heavy meals; Over exertion after Snehapana & Vamana; Sudden change from cold to heat or heat to cold without following the rules of gradual change; Improper administration of Snehapana and Panchakarma Procedures.

sections.title: Follow Up
sections.content: Follow Up: Once in every 15 days or as needed, for effective management of the condition. Frequent and long term follow up is needed to monitor psoriasis patients to prevent recurrence and monitor remissions and exacerbations, if any. Strict Pathyaapathya are to be continued for a period equal to or two times the total panchakarma treatment period during follow up. Naimittika rasayanas should be given on follow up.

sections.title: Referral Criteria
sections.content: Level 1 Referral Criteria: A PASI score of 5 to 10 is considered moderate disease, and a score more than 10 is considered severe with substantial impact of quality of life and daily living; Generalized pustular psoriasis or erythrodermic psoriasis patients can be referred to a higher centre for specific management; Uncontrolled co-morbidities; Evidence of an increase in severity/complications; Diagnostic uncertainty. Level 2 Referral Criteria: Same as mentioned earlier at level 1, plus Failure of acute exacerbation to respond to initial medical management; In erythrodermic patients with generalized pustular psoriasis, patients with febrile and unstable vitals or secondary infections; Cases with prominent joint damage and marked functional impairment; Uncontrolled complications such as Cardiovascular disease, Cancer, HIV, metabolic syndrome, psychiatric illness or hyperuricaemia; Any other complications that threaten the life of the patient. Level 3 Referral Criteria: Same as mentioned earlier at level 2, plus Other modalities can be considered depending on the case.

sections.title: Level 2 & Level 3 Treatment
sections.content: Level 2: (CHC/Small hospitals (10-20 bedded hospitals with basic facilities such as routine investigation, X-ray). Clinical Diagnosis: The case referred from Level 1, or a fresh case must be evaluated thoroughly for any complications. Identification of patient specific etiopathological factors (nidana) in diet and lifestyle, classification based on dosha involvement and staging of the disease based on dhatu involvement should be done to plan the treatment accordingly. Investigations: Complete blood count/ ESR; Renal function Test, liver function test; Fasting lipids, glucose, and thyroid functions; Complete urine examination; High sensitivity C-reactive protein; Serum electrolytes; X-ray of affected Joints (Psoriatic arthritis); Tests for Biologics is referred to a specialized tertiary level center. Management: OPD/IPD level management: In addition to the management mentioned in Level 1, staging and classification of the psoriasis based on dhatus affected and doshas involved should be done at level 2 to determine the prognosis and mode of management. The sadhya (curable) Kustha roga affecting only rasa, rakta and mamsa can be treated at OPD level and yapya (managed with strict diet and regimen but not completely curable) Kustha roga which affects medodhatu should be treated in a hospital with constant follow up to prevent recurrence. The cases in which only alpadoshatwa, is present may be treated at the OPD level with identification of specific nidanas, nidanaparivarjana, vicharanasnehapana, shodhana, naimittikarasayana and sesha dosha shamana. When the psoriatic lesions are limited to skin, it can be treated under the line of treatment of Kustha rogas and raktavritavata. When Shodhana is done, the bala of the patient should be taken into consideration. In vata predominant conditions, snehapana and anulomana with Kusthaharasnehas are advised and madhyama and pravarashodhana are avoided. Vamana is indicated in psoriasis with kapha predominance and those affecting upper parts of the body (example, scalp psoriasis). Virechana is indicated in pitta predominance and those affecting lower parts of the body (example, pustular psoriasis, inverse psoriasis). Shardikavirechana can be employed for shodhana of pitta in September month where predominant pitta vitiation is involved. Vasantika vamana can be employed for shodhana of kapha in February-March months where aggravation of kapha is seen. Madhutailikavasti indicated for Kustha and Prameha can be given in psoriatic arthropathy which has become chronic and shows signs of vata pitta or vata involvement. Nasya can be effectively used in psoriasis affecting the scalp. It also reduces anxiety and stress and also improves sleep. If there is bahudoshatwa, the patient may be admitted in Level 2 hospital for Achasnehapana, madhyama to pravarashodhana (vamana and virechana), rasayana, with constant monitoring and observation. When the joints are involved in psoriatic arthropathy, vatarakta and vatavyadhi line of treatment are applicable. Level 3: Ayush hospitals are attached with teaching institutions, District Level/ Integrated/ State Ayush Hospitals, Tertiary care allopathic hospitals having Ayush facilities, and multiple departments/ facilities for diagnosis and interventions. Additional facilities like dieticians, counselling, and physiotherapy must be provided. Clinical Diagnosis: Same as Levels 1& 2. Confirm diagnosis and severity with the help of investigations such as skin biopsy (only done for cases in which clinical diagnosis is not clear), Further investigations like inflammatory bio markers, ECHO, MRI, CT scan, and chemical analysis of uric acid renal stones, Fibroscan (to detect early liver damage in patients with a history of methotrexate used for 2-3 years and alcohol consumption) etc may be advised as per individual case needs. Management: The treatment strategy planning at level 3 is also based on dosha dominance and includes purificatory therapies for bahudosha Kustha, and subsequent rasayana medicines for strengthening the purified dhathu, as mentioned in Level 2. In the case of madhyama dosha or alpa dosha Kustha, shamanoushadhi will be utilized as per dosha dominance and dhatu involvement. The medicines that can be utilized in the treatment of psoriasis is given in Table No: 9. The treatment of psoriasis will not be complete without nidana parivarjana or identification and avoidance of etiological factors which may vary from individual-to-individual. Management of psoriatic complications: In metabolic complications associated with psoriasis including metabolic syndrome, NAFLD, anemia and liver cirrhosis, patolamooladi kwatha, patolakaturohinyadi kwatha, vasa guduchyadi kwatha, arogyavardhini vati can be advocated. In psychiatric complications associated with psoriasis, the snehana samanoushadha including kalyanaka ghrita, maha kalyanaka ghrita; manasa mitravataka, takra sirodhara etc can be advocated.

sections.title: General Instructions
sections.content: Psoriasis is a chronic, recurrent condition. Long-term follow-up is needed to prevent recurrence and monitor remissions and exacerbations. Patients should be educated about the non-contagious nature of psoriasis. Stress management is important as stress can exacerbate psoriasis. Patients should avoid known triggers including certain medications (beta blockers, lithium, synthetic antimalarials, NSAIDs, Tetracycline, ACE inhibitors, interferon and antifungals).
